P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, into domiciliary (USD and other foreign-currency) accounts at Nigerian banks. CBN's new Foreign Exchange Manual (4th edition) took effect on 1 June 2026. Ordinary domiciliary account holders get 'unfettered and unrestricted access' to their funds without prior regulatory approval, and Form A is no longer required for remittances from ordinary domiciliary accounts. Banks still verify the purpose. Export-proceeds domiciliary accounts are stricter: no cash withdrawals, and access depends on transaction documents. CBN says export proceeds must be repatriated and credited to exporters' domiciliary accounts within 180 days for non-oil exports, and since 8 January 2025 extensions are suspended. CBN has also said it won't force holders to convert domiciliary balances to naira.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual selling digital products or services register a business? How (sole proprietor), cost, online?
L1_registration.answer: Only if you trade under a business name. Under CAMA 2020 s.814, an individual with a place of business in Nigeria must register a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) when the name is anything other than their true surname plus forenames or initials. Registration is needed before starting, or within 28 days of starting under that name. Trading under your own name needs no registration, and Paystack's 'Starter Business' route works without CAC registration (P3). Banks generally require a registered name to open a business account, and Payoneer's Kuda route needs CAC registration (P5).

L2_tax_id.question: Tax identification number requirement and how to get it
L2_tax_id.answer: Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (in force since 1 January 2026), every taxable person must register with the relevant tax authority and get a Taxpayer Identification number ('Tax ID'). The tax authority must issue one on request, and can register people who failed to apply. Banks and other financial-services providers must make sure every taxable person gives them a Tax ID. The Nigeria Revenue Service handles companies, non-residents and others; individuals' income tax is administered by their State's tax authority.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: How residents' foreign-sourced or digital income is taxed
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Nigeria Tax Act 2025 (in force since 1 January 2026; it repealed the Personal Income Tax Act and others): a resident individual's income is taxable in Nigeria wherever it arises, whether or not it is brought into Nigeria. Freelance and online income earned from abroad is therefore taxable. Rates for individuals on taxable income: first ₦800,000 at 0%, next ₦2.2m at 15%, next ₦9m at 18%, next ₦13m at 21%, next ₦25m at 23%, and above ₦50m at 25%. Profits or gains from digital asset transactions are explicitly chargeable.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported services and digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Nigeria Tax Act 2025: VAT is 7.5% on taxable supplies (s.147). Exported services, exported goods (excluding oil and gas) and exported incorporeal property such as IP and digital rights are zero-rated (s.186). A 'small company' is one with gross turnover of ₦100m or less and fixed assets up to ₦250m. The VAT registration or charging threshold for individuals and small businesses was not verified (see notes).

D1_id_document.question: Name of the national identity document residents use for identity checks
D1_id_document.answer: The National Identification Number (NIN), an 11-digit number from the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC). W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving). Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Card payments on your own site through Paystack (a Stripe company). Stripe lists this country under its extended network. (6) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (7) Local official channel: Receive into an ordinary domiciliary (USD) account. Under the CBN FX Manual in force from 1 June 2026, holders have unrestricted access without prior approval (P1/P2). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
